## Why this model, why this is a first attempt

The other services in this project's pipeline arrived as pre-computed InVEST outputs — earlier
work, by Becky and collaborators, that this project only ever post-processed. Seasonal Water
Yield (SWY) is different: **nobody has run InVEST SWY at anything approaching global scale
before**, on this project or, as far as a systematic literature review found, anywhere else. That
is not a rhetorical claim; it follows from a real precedent review.

## Precedent review

Every InVEST SWY application found in the literature is watershed- or country-scale: a West
Bengal (India) study, a two-basin Peru/Myanmar study [@hamel2020], and UK-catchment validation
work. No published global-scale application exists. The closest analogue to a "global" precedent
isn't InVEST-specific at all — it's GCN250 [@jaafar2019], a global gridded curve-number product
that solves the same underlying problem (curve number varies by land cover and geography, no
single number works everywhere) as a general hydrology product, independent of InVEST's own
workflow.

Reading @hamel2020 in full (not just the abstract) changes the framing in two ways worth being
explicit about:

1. **Neither of their case studies derived CN or Kc from literature tables cold.** Peru reused CN
   values from an existing calibrated SWAT model of that exact basin, built years earlier for a
   payments-for-ecosystem-services program. Myanmar reused CN/Kc from an existing national
   ecosystem-service assessment [@mandle2017]. The operational lesson: search for an existing
   calibrated hydrologic study or ecosystem-service assessment covering a representative watershed
   in each biome that needs a correction, rather than deriving values from cover-type tables from
   scratch.
2. **Model reliability appears to degrade at large basin scale, and their largest basin was only
   114,000 km².** Their own guidance recommends caution with absolute values "in new geographies,"
   with relative baseflow results in basins under 10,000 km² best supported by their validation
   data. A genuinely global run is planetary scale — several orders of magnitude beyond anything
   validated in this literature, InVEST-specific or otherwise. **Whether "one global run" is even
   the right framing is a live open question**, not a settled premise — a basin-by-basin or
   regional-mosaic approach (closer to what Hamel et al. actually did: two separate basin-scale
   applications, not one global one) may be the more defensible framing than a single
   planetary-scale run.

The quickflow method itself traces to @guswa2018, validated against 544 US watersheds — a reminder
that the model's core empirical grounding is American in origin, not tropical or global, independent
of any input-data question.

## Which layer of Rich's pipeline this project actually uses

Worth stating precisely, since "Rich's pipeline" collapses three distinct things that are easy to
conflate mid-conversation:

1. **Vanilla InVEST** (`natcap.invest.seasonal_water_yield`) — the public, stock model. **Not used
   anywhere in this project.**
2. **`inspring`** (`github.com/springinnovate/inspring`) — Rich's extended research fork of the SWY
   model. Same core science as stock InVEST, but adds one capability stock InVEST lacks: it accepts
   **direct raster overrides** for CN and Kc (`cn_a/b/c/d_path`, `kc_1...12_path`) in addition to the
   standard lucode-indexed CSV biophysical table. **This is what this project calls** — directly, via
   `inspring.seasonal_water_yield.execute()`.
3. **`swy_global`** (`github.com/springinnovate/swy_global`) — Rich's *orchestration layer* on top of
   `inspring`, built for running SWY at planetary scale: it splits a watershed vector into per-basin
   jobs, pre-warps every input to each job's local UTM zone, runs each basin through `inspring` in
   parallel via TaskGraph, and stitches results into one continuous global mosaic. **Not used by this
   project's own test runs** (Borneo, and the Philippines comparison below) — each is called as a
   single AOI, directly against `inspring`, with no batching or stitching. `swy_global` is the
   long-term target architecture for an eventual real global run, not what produced any result in
   this document.

One-line version for a live conversation: *this project uses Rich's `inspring` engine directly, with
inputs built by hand rather than through his `swy_global` global-run machinery, and runs each test
basin as a single watershed job.*

## Model inputs — current status

| Input | Status (2026-09-10) |
|---|---|
| AOI / watershed vector | Built — `borneo_aoi.gpkg`, dissolved from HydroBASINS Australia/Oceania [@lehner2013] level-6 units, 1.4% area error against Borneo's known extent |
| DEM | Sourced and verified — SRTMGL3 [@farr2007], 90m. Elevation range -91–4041m against a known high point of 4095m (Mt. Kinabalu) |
| Routing parameters | Rich's `swy_global.ini` defaults (`THRESHOLD_FLOW_ACCUMULATION=1000`, `ALPHA_M=0.083333`, `BETA_I=1`, `GAMMA=1`) |
| LULC | ESA CCI 1992 / Copernicus C3S 2020, 300m, already used elsewhere in this pipeline |
| Soil hydrologic group | HYSOGs250m [@ross2018] |
| Monthly precipitation | Sourced and verified — CHIRPS [@funk2015], 2020, ~5.5km |
| Monthly ET0 | Sourced and verified — TerraClimate `pet` [@abatzoglou2018], 2020, ~4km, ASCE Penman-Monteith corrected for CO2 |
| Rain events table | Derivable from CHIRPS daily via a working script; precip is in hand, derivation not yet run |
| Curve number (CN) base | GCN250 [@jaafar2019] |
| NDVI (feeds Kc) | Sourced and verified — MOD13A3 [@didan2021], full 2000–2026 record |
| `root_depth` | Required by the `inspring` interface but confirmed dead code in this fork — a placeholder raster satisfies it |

## Why two climate data sources (CHIRPS and TerraClimate) — not a substitution

Worth stating plainly, since it's an easy thing to misremember as "one source was missing
something so we swapped to the other": **CHIRPS and TerraClimate are not alternatives for the
same variable.** They feed two different model inputs that InVEST SWY requires simultaneously,
not one input satisfied two ways:

- **CHIRPS** [@funk2015] → `precip_dir` (monthly precipitation). CHIRPS is a **precipitation-only
  product** — it has no evapotranspiration variable at all, by design and scope, not because of a
  data gap.
- **TerraClimate** `pet` [@abatzoglou2018] → `et0_dir` (reference evapotranspiration). InVEST
  SWY's water balance needs precipitation and reference-ET as two separate monthly raster stacks:
  quickflow depends on precipitation and CN; actual evapotranspiration depends on reference-ET,
  Kc, and leftover precipitation after quickflow. CHIRPS was never a candidate for the ET0 role —
  it simply doesn't produce that variable. TerraClimate was sourced specifically to fill this
  separate, always-required input, found and vetted for the first time in this project on
  2026-09-10 (see `docs/swy/research_notes.md`).

**There is a real, separate CHIRPS limitation — but it's about a different input, and doesn't
apply to either test basin.** CHIRPS's real spatial coverage is roughly 50°S–50°N. That matters
for the **rain-events table** (`08_build_rain_events_table.py`'s eventual real derivation, not
the placeholder currently in use) if this project ever attempts a true global run — daily CHIRPS
data wouldn't cover high-latitude basins. It is irrelevant for Borneo and the Philippines, both
well within CHIRPS's coverage. Don't conflate this genuine future-global-run caveat with the
precipitation-vs-ET0 question above; they're unrelated limitations of the same product.

## How CN and Kc actually get fed to the model

InVEST's documented convention is a lucode-indexed biophysical table — one CSV row per land-cover
class, columns for `CN_A`/`CN_B`/`CN_C`/`CN_D` and `Kc_1`...`Kc_12`. `inspring`
(`github.com/springinnovate/inspring`, Rich's implementation) additionally accepts **direct raster
overrides** per factor (`cn_a/b/c/d_path`, `kc_1...12_path`, `root_depth_path`) — confirmed by
reading the code directly, not inferred from documentation. When every factor is raster-overridden,
`lulc_raster_path` itself becomes unnecessary.

This project uses the raster-override path for both CN and Kc, because both underlying products are
inherently continuous already — GCN250 is a per-pixel raster, and the NDVI-Kc regression below
computes a value per pixel per month. Routing either through a shared, class-based lucode scheme
first would discard resolution, not add anything. To be clear about what is and is not novel here:
continuous, gridded parameterization is the default in most physically-based distributed hydrology
models (VIC, PCR-GLOBWB, and similar land-surface models are raster-native from the start) — it is
InVEST's table-based convention that is the special case, a design choice suited to its usual
land-use-scenario comparison use case. The raster-override path is best understood as `inspring`'s
own engineering solution for making a genuinely large-extent run of a table-oriented model
tractable, not a novel modeling idea introduced by this project. Whether this specific path is
something other InVEST users rely on, or a bespoke solution built for this project's own global-run
ambitions, is an open question worth asking Rich directly rather than assuming either way.

### What the Borneo run actually did, vs. this document's target architecture

The paragraph above describes the *intended, architecturally preferable* setup. **The Borneo run
itself did not use it.** It used the traditional CSV `biophysical_table_path` route (lucode → CN_A-D,
Kc_1-12), not the raster-override args — a deliberate, documented, pragmatic call under time
pressure (the CSV path was already fully built; the raster-override path wasn't, yet), not an
oversight. Documented in `Python_scripts/swy_borneo_run/README.md` and in
`09_run_swy_borneo.py`'s own docstring. **Say this plainly rather than letting it surface as an
inconsistency mid-conversation**: table-based for this first pass; raster-override remains the
correct next step, not yet taken.

### Two CN tables — a real distinction, not duplication

`data/swy/shared/cn_tables/` holds two CSVs that are easy to conflate:

- **`gcn250_pft_base_cn_table.csv`** — CN values keyed by **PFT** (Plant Functional Type: "Tree
  Broadleaf Evergreen," "Shrub Deciduous," "Natural grass," etc.), with an explicit `NEH630_basis`
  column. This is GCN250's own **native classification** — its authors assigned CN values to NRCS
  NEH-630 hydrologic-cover categories, which are expressed as PFTs, not as any particular land-cover
  product's classes.
- **`gcn250_esa_lc_cn_table.csv`** — the same CN values, **crosswalked onto ESA CCI/Copernicus C3S
  land-cover codes** (`LC_ID`: 10 = rainfed cropland, 50 = broadleaf evergreen tree cover, etc.) —
  the actual class codes present in this project's LULC raster.

**Only the second table is read by the pipeline** (`07_build_biophysical_table.py` joins it by
`lucode`). The PFT table is upstream reference material — it explains *why* the ESA-LC values are
what they are — but nothing in the pipeline loads it directly, and **no PFT raster exists or is used
anywhere**; PFT is a classification scheme inside one CN lookup table, never spatial data in this
project.

(A third, unrelated file that can confuse this further if it comes up: `swy_global`'s own repo ships
`base_data/biophysical_template_PH.csv`, a schema-example biophysical table Rich included — named
for the Philippines by coincidence, unrelated to Becky's Philippines model run discussed below. Not
a third real CN table in play here.)

## Curve number: methodology and the biome-patch decision

InVEST's own documentation is explicit that there is no defensible global shortcut for CN — it
depends on soil group, cover type, and moisture condition, and region-specific values are preferred
over blanket defaults [@usda_neh630_2007]. **GCN250** [@jaafar2019] solves the bulk of this: a
purpose-built, peer-reviewed global CN product combining land cover and soil hydrologic group
[@ross2018], with three antecedent-runoff-condition variants. Its own authors are candid that it
differentiates by land-cover granularity, not by region-specific values *within* one land-cover
class, and that the underlying method is least validated in forested/humid tropical environments.

**Recommended approach: GCN250 as baseline, targeted biome-level correction on top.** This maps onto
a short list of this pipeline's WWF biome classes, not all sixteen: Tropical & Subtropical Moist
Broadleaf Forests, Mangroves, and Flooded Grasslands & Savannas are the priority candidates for a
literature-sourced correction layered on the GCN250 baseline. This is not a hypothetical
refinement — @hamel2020's own sensitivity analysis found quickflow changing by **factors of
10–13×** between antecedent-moisture-condition CN settings in a single basin. CN is close to the
dominant source of variance in this model's output.

Per @hamel2020's own precedent (search for an existing calibrated study rather than deriving from
cover-type tables cold):

| Biome | Status |
|---|---|
| Tropical moist broadleaf forest | Real candidates found [@calero2021; @fabrega2012], both confirming the standard method overestimates runoff under tropical conditions. Patch is buildable. |
| Flooded grasslands & savannas | Direct hit: @oliveira2016, measured CN from Brazilian Cerrado (undisturbed savanna CN ≈ 81.2 on soil group B) — the closest ecological analogue to the Colombian Llanos/Orinoquía. @nogales2021 is valuable regional precedent but is **not** a CN source (different model, no vegetation-based parameterization) — don't conflate the two. |
| Mangroves | No usable literature found after three search passes. These are tide-flooded systems — CN's rainfall-runoff premise doesn't describe what drives water movement here. Leaning toward documenting this as a structural limitation of the CN method itself, not a literature gap to keep searching for. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

## Crop coefficient: methodology

The governing relationship, per FAO-56 [@allen1998]:

$$ET_c = K_c \times ET_0$$

where $ET_0$ is reference evapotranspiration from climate data alone, and $K_c$ is a unitless
multiplier reflecting what's actually growing on a pixel. `inspring` computes this internally per
month as $PET_m = K_{c,m} \times ET0_m$.

FAO-56's own tables don't solve this globally: they're built for managed crops with defined growth
stages, calibrated against Northern-Hemisphere crop calendars — most global land area is not
cropland, and has no "planting date" for that framework to apply to. The three-way split used here:

- **Cropland**: FAO-56 tables [@allen1998], adapted with region-correct crop-calendar timing (the
  reference tool's built-in defaults are Northern-Hemisphere only, and does not have a native entry
  for oil palm — an open question for whichever cropland is actually dominant in a given AOI).
- **Non-crop vegetation** (forest, grassland, shrubland — most of global land area): the validated
  NDVI regression from @kamble2013, calibrated against AmeriFlux eddy-covariance flux-tower
  measurements across multiple vegetation types ($r^2 = 0.90$–$0.91$):

  $$K_c = 1.457 \times NDVI - 0.1725$$

  Corroborated by multiple follow-up studies through 2025, including one Sentinel-2 study
  reporting an even tighter fit [@grapevine_kc_2025]. This is an empirical, statistical
  relationship, not a mechanistic one — it assumes the same linear slope holds across vegetation
  physiologies and regions the original flux towers didn't sample. That is a real simplifying
  assumption, not a proven universal law, though the same category of assumption GCN250 makes for
  CN, and one repeatedly replicated rather than a one-off finding.
- **Non-vegetated** (water, wetlands, bare soil, built): fixed values from InVEST's own guidance
  [@invest_userguide_2026].

**Open problem, raised directly by Rich (2026-09-11), not yet resolved:** Kamble et al. was
calibrated **entirely on agricultural crops** (US High Plains cropping systems) — not forest,
grassland, or any natural vegetation. Applying it to forest pixels (the majority of both Borneo's
and the Philippines' land area) is an extrapolation outside its validated domain, not a like-for-
like use. Rich's specific concern: NDVI saturates in dense canopy, so a **linear** fit calibrated
on agricultural NDVI ranges may *underestimate* Kc once extrapolated to saturated forest NDVI.

**Independent check attempted** [@corbari2017]: four real eddy-covariance sites (pasture, deciduous
forest, evergreen conifer forest — none tropical) measured Kc directly, no NDVI involved. Result:
measured forest Kc came in **lower** than standard FAO/LAI-based assumptions, not higher (evergreen
conifer Kc≈0.17–0.20, deciduous Kc≈0.43–0.51, vs. FAO's ~0.78–0.9). Even the highest of these
real-measured values is less than half what our Kamble regression predicts at forest-level NDVI
(~0.85–0.90 → Kc≈1.07–1.14). **This does not confirm Rich's underestimation hypothesis — if
anything it points the other way** — but it's temperate-forest data, not tropical, so it doesn't
settle the question either. **No tropical-forest-specific source found yet.** Glenn et al. (2011,
*Hydrological Processes*) explicitly covers "natural ecosystems" and is the next thing to check —
not yet obtained (blocked behind a paywall as of this writing).

**Update: Glenn et al. (2011)** [@glenn2011] **read in full — confirms Rich's mechanism is real,
even though Corbari's numbers didn't point the same direction.** Two concrete findings:

1. **NDVI saturates around LAI≈3; EVI and SAVI don't**, and are established in this literature as
   the better choice for exactly this reason — several cited studies found MODIS EVI
   significantly better correlated with ground-measured ET than MODIS NDVI across land-cover
   types. Kamble's regression uses plain NDVI. **Switching to EVI (same MOD13A3.061 product,
   different layer — no new data source needed) is a concrete, low-cost improvement**, not yet
   made.
2. **A real tropical rainforest precedent exists**: Juarez et al. (2008), Amazonia, MODIS
   EVI + net radiation, r²=0.72–0.86 against flux towers. Not yet obtained/read — the next actual
   source to chase, and the first one so far that's tropical-forest-specific rather than temperate.

General accuracy bound from this literature: flux-tower-calibrated Kc-VI methods run
**10–30% RMSE** against measured ET (vs. 5–10% for lysimeter-calibrated single agricultural
crops) — worth citing as a realistic uncertainty range rather than treating any single Kc number
as precise.

**Bottom line: the mechanism Rich raised is real and independently documented; the direction and
size of its effect on Borneo/Philippines specifically is still unknown.** Concrete next steps, not
yet done: switch NDVI→EVI in the Kc pipeline; obtain and read Juarez et al. (2008) for an actual
tropical-forest calibration reference. Don't present current forest Kc as validated until then.

The three are merged per-pixel via a land-cover mask (crop / non-crop-vegetation / non-vegetated) —
a much smaller artifact than a full lucode-indexed biophysical table, since CN and Kc are otherwise
raster-overridden as described above.

**In practice, both Borneo and the Philippines test runs skip this three-way split entirely** and
apply the NDVI regression uniformly to every vegetated class, cropland included — the documented,
deliberate simplification in `07_build_biophysical_table.py` for both regions, since neither has
region-correct FAO-56 crop-calendar timing built yet. **The cost of this simplification is not the
same in both places, worth being precise about rather than treating "same code, same caveat" as
"equally defensible":**

- **Borneo's cropland is predominantly oil palm (rainfed)** — the gap there is a *calendar*
  mismatch: FAO-56's built-in defaults are Northern-Hemisphere and don't have a native oil palm
  entry at all, but the underlying crop is still a normal, non-flooded, continuously-vegetated
  plantation crop that an NDVI-based Kc curve describes reasonably.
- **The Philippines' cropland includes substantially more irrigated/flooded rice paddy** — the
  ESA-LC CN crosswalk already distinguishes this at the CN level (class 10, rainfed cropland,
  CN 57–78 vs. class 20, irrigated/post-flooding cropland, CN 61–80 — see the two-CN-tables note
  above), but Kc does **not** make the same distinction; the same NDVI-based formula applies
  regardless. This is a *regime* mismatch, not just a calendar one: flooded paddy behaves
  hydrologically much closer to open water during its flooded phase than to the general upland
  vegetation types the @kamble2013 regression was calibrated against (AmeriFlux towers, not
  paddy-specific). **This makes the shared simplification a weaker approximation for the
  Philippines than for Borneo**, specifically wherever paddy rice dominates the cropland fraction —
  worth stating plainly rather than letting "we did the same thing as Borneo" imply the same
  confidence level.

## Rain events

Not directly available from any source — derived by counting days with more than 0.1mm of rainfall
per month from a daily precipitation product. CHIRPS [@funk2015] has the necessary daily
granularity; a working script (`calculate_average_monthly_events.py`) already exists. Rain-day
frequency genuinely varies by climate zone, which is InVEST's own stated reason for offering a
"climate zone" advanced option as an alternative to a single global rain-events table.

## Output variables: what each raster actually means

Pulled directly from `inspring`'s source (`seasonal_water_yield.py` and the Cython core
`seasonal_water_yield_core.pyx` — `calculate_local_recharge`, `route_baseflow_sum`), not inferred
from filenames. Two of these (QF, AET) are computed **independently at each pixel**; the rest
depend on **DEM-derived flow routing** — that distinction is exactly why QF and AET were
byte-identical between Borneo's crashed and complete runs while `L_sum` was not (see
`research_notes.md`'s 2026-09-11 entries).

| Variable | File | What it is | Depends on routing? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `QF` / `qf_1`...`qf_12` | `QF.tif`, monthly `qf_*.tif` | Quickflow (surface runoff) — computed per pixel per month straight from CN and rainfall statistics via the closed-form stochastic-rainfall expression [@guswa2018]. | No |
| `AET` | `aet.tif` | Actual evapotranspiration — `min(PET_m, P_m − QF_m + baseflow contribution)` per month, summed. | No |
| `L` | `L.tif` | Local recharge — the water left over locally once quickflow and AET are subtracted from precipitation; "how much water could recharge groundwater at this pixel." | No |
| `L_avail` | `L_avail.tif` | `L` capped by the model parameter `gamma` (Eq. 8: `L_avail = min(gamma·L, L)`) — the portion of local recharge actually available to contribute downstream. Borneo's run used `gamma=1`, so `L_avail = L` there. | No |
| `L_sum` | `L_sum.tif` | **Flow-accumulated** `L` — every pixel's `L` value routed downhill along the DEM-derived Multiple-Flow-Direction (MFD) network and summed over its upstream contributing area: "total upstream recharge draining through this pixel." | **Yes** — this is the layer with Borneo's anomaly, because flow accumulation is exactly the kind of calculation that blows up at DEM sinks or flat, tidally-ambiguous coastal terrain. |
| `L_sum_avail` | `L_sum_avail.tif` | The same flow-accumulation idea applied to the *available* (bounded) recharge rather than raw `L` — feeds the baseflow-index calculation. | Yes |
| `B` | `B.tif` | Baseflow — the final per-pixel routed output, computed from `L`, `L_avail`, and `L_sum` along the same MFD network, referenced against the stream raster. This is the model's actual "how much of the accumulated recharge shows up as sustained streamflow" answer. | Yes |
| `B_sum` | `B_sum.tif` | Upslope-accumulated `B` — routed the same way as `L_sum`, one step further downstream. | Yes |
| `Vri` | `vri.tif` | `L / (AOI-wide sum of L)` — a per-pixel share of total recharge, used for aggregation, not a routed quantity itself. | No |
| `aggregated_results_swy*.shp` | — | The final watershed-scale rollup (e.g. `qb` = aggregate baseflow, `vri_sum`) — the very last computational step; its presence with a real value is the strongest single signal a run actually completed. | Yes (depends on everything above) |

**Practical implication for comparing against any external SWY output (Becky's Philippines run
included)**: `QF` and `AET` are the safest pixel-level layers to compare directly, since they don't
depend on routing quality. `L_sum`, `L_sum_avail`, `B`, and `B_sum` are only as trustworthy as the
DEM/flow-direction step — compare these with the routing-anomaly caveat in mind, not as
unconditionally reliable ground truth.

## Test design: Borneo

**Decided with Becky, 2026-09-09.** The actual goal is a global run; running end-to-end on a real
basin is a necessary check, not the goal itself. The real question this test answers is whether
this project's own CN/Kc parametrization — built from public, peer-reviewed global products rather
than a hand-built regional table — is robust enough to trust at that scale. Borneo, not Indonesia as
a whole, is the test case: the large, single landmass that allows a real-scale test without the
added complication of Indonesia's thousands of small islands.

Two things represent a real shift from where this research started, worth stating plainly:

- **The mangrove/flooded-savannas CN gap is not a blocker for this round.** Resolving that patch
  before testing was this project's own caution, not a condition Becky set.
- **Rigorous validation against a published result is not the priority for this round either** —
  confirming the pipeline runs end-to-end on a real basin matters more right now than proving
  numerical agreement with an external benchmark.

The original, stricter framing — reproducing a known published result closely enough to trust
further scaling — was to test against one of @hamel2020's own basins (Peru or Myanmar), since they
have published, granular output to check a result against. Peru's CN came from an existing
calibrated SWAT model [@abbaspour2019 gives the class of tool, not this specific calibration];
Myanmar's from an existing ecosystem-service assessment [@mandle2017]. That reasoning remains
scientifically sound and worth returning to for a rigor-focused validation later — it just isn't
what this round is for.

## Open research questions

- **Is "one global run" the right framing at all**, or should this proceed as a set of
  basin-by-basin/regional-mosaic runs combined afterward — closer to what @hamel2020 actually did?
  Not resolved; named explicitly rather than assumed away.
- **The mangrove CN gap** — is documenting it as a structural limitation of the curve-number method
  (not merely an unfilled literature gap) the right final position?
- **Is the `inspring` raster-override path a known pattern elsewhere**, or specific engineering
  built for this project's own use case? Worth asking Rich directly.
- **Oil palm and FAO-56** — cropland Kc assumes a native FAO-56 entry exists; it does not for oil
  palm specifically, the crop most likely to actually dominate Borneo's cropland fraction.
